Numerous researchers examined trends in SRCs across multiple sports at the high school level. Lincoln and col - leagues4 examined high school boys’ and girls’ sports be- tween the 1997/1998 and 2007/2008 seasons, with football exhibiting the highest incidence rate followed by girls’ soccer, boys’ wrestling, and girls’ basketball. Over the 11- year period, the incidence of SRCs increased by 4.2-fold, with an average annual increase of 15.5%.4 Another study examining high school trends in SRCs found a 2.3-fold increase in cases between 2004/2005 and 2014/2015.6 In contrast, Chun and colleagues7 examined trends in Hawai- ian high school SRCs and reported no significant trends over the 6-year study period (2011–2017). Due to these inconsistent findings and increasing participation rates,1 it is crucial to analyze trends in high school SRCs to guide prevention efforts and ensure the safety of adolescents. Prior studies indicate that high school girls participat - ing in sports comparable to those played by boys have a 2-times-higher SRC injury rate. 3,8 Notably, research - ers consistently found a higher SRC injury rate in girls’ soccer, basketball, and softball versus comparable boys’ sports.3,8–11 Additionally, research indicates that SRCs constituted a higher proportion of all high school injuries among girls compared to boys.10 Recent evidence suggests that boys and girls exhibit differences in mechanism of SRC in comparable activities. 12 Girls more often incur their SRCs due to player-to–playing surface or player-to- equipment contact, whereas boys sustained the majority of their SRCs due to player-to-player contact.10,12,13 How- ever, with the global pandemic as well as decreasing and increasing sports participation over the past decade, it is important to continuously examine and document trends in SRCs between boys’ and girls’ high school sports. We calculated the clinical incidence of SRC, dividing the number of SRCs by the number of athletic participants multiplied by 100 player-seasons, and presented data as 95% CIs. We conducted clinical incidence analyses over- all, and for boys’ and girls’ sports separately, and stratified by each academic year and also independently for each sport. We included data from 2019/2020 and 2020/2021; however, due to the COVID-19 pandemic we counsel cau- tion regarding interpretations. We calculated the overall clinical incidence among all sports, and for boys’ and girls’ sports with and without academic years impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic. Wiebe, PhD,1,3 and Tracey Covassin, PhD2 Departments of 1Emergency Medicine and 3Epidemiology, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor; and 2Department of Kinesiology, Michigan State University, East Lansing, Michigan OBJECTIVE Epidemiology provides fundamental opportunities to protect student-athlete health. The goal of this study was to describe the epidemiology of sport-related concussion (SRC) across 8 years (2015/2016–2022/2023) and com - pare boys’ and girls’ sports for SRC incidence and SRC mechanisms. METHODS This was a retrospective cohort study performed using a statewide high school head injury surveillance sys- tem of high school student-athletes (n = 2,182,128; boys, n = 1,267,389; girls, n = 914,739). Exposures of interest included study year and boys and girls in comparable sports. Clinical incidence was calculated by dividing SRC counts in each sport by the number of participants per 100 player-seasons and presented with 95% CIs. The 2019/2020 and 2020/2021 data were included in the analysis, however caution is warranted due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Clinical incidence ratios (CIRs) were estimated for sex-comparable sports, and significance was determined if 95% CIs excluded 1.00. The authors compared mechanism of injury in boys’ and girls’ comparable sports with chi-square analyses (p < 0.05). RESULTS Among 25,482 total SRCs, the overall clinical incidence of SRC for all boys and girls was 1.17 (95% CI 1.15–1.18) per 100 player-seasons across all years. Across all years, the overall clinical incidence in boys’ sports was 1.34 (95% CI 1.32–1.36) per 100 player-seasons, and 0.93 (95% CI 0.91–0.95) per 100 player-seasons in girls’ sports. Boys’ sports with the highest clinical incidence included football, ice hockey, and wrestling. Girls’ sports with the highest clinical incidence included basketball, soccer, lacrosse, competitive cheer, and gymnastics. Girls consistently had higher SRC rates relative to boys for baseball/softball, basketball, and soccer (CIR range 1.65 [95% CI 1.41–1.93] to 3.32 [95% CI 2.67–4.16]). Girls had lower SRC in lacrosse in 2015/2016 (CIR 0.63, 95% CI 0.40–0.97); no difference in 2016/2017– 2020/2021, but had higher clinical incidence in 2021/2022 (CIR 1.69, 95% CI 1.18–2.44) relative to boys. In boys the most common mechanism of SRC occurred from person-to-person contact (n = 8752, 62.8%), whereas girls commonly sustained SRC from person-to-object contact (n = 2369, 33.4%) and from person-to-person contact (n = 2368, 33.4%). There were significant associations between boys’ versus girls’ sports and mechanism of injury within baseball/softball (χ2 = 12.71, p = 0.005); basketball (χ2 = 36.47, p < 0.001); lacrosse (χ2 = 185.15, p < 0.001); and soccer (χ2 = 122.70, p < 0.001).

Neurosurg Focus Volume 57 • July 2024 2 cer and basketball have the highest SRC rates at the high school level.3–5 Basic epidemiology and investigations to identify patterns are essential to identify the preventive ef- fect that could be achieved if countermeasures were used to safeguard the health of this vulnerable population. Numerous researchers examined trends in SRCs across multiple sports at the high school level. Lincoln and col - leagues4 examined high school boys’ and girls’ sports be- tween the 1997/1998 and 2007/2008 seasons, with football exhibiting the highest incidence rate followed by girls’ soccer, boys’ wrestling, and girls’ basketball. Over the 11- year period, the incidence of SRCs increased by 4.2-fold, with an average annual increase of 15.5%.4 Another study examining high school trends in SRCs found a 2.3-fold increase in cases between 2004/2005 and 2014/2015.6 In contrast, Chun and colleagues7 examined trends in Hawai- ian high school SRCs and reported no significant trends over the 6-year study period (2011–2017). Due to these inconsistent findings and increasing participation rates,1 it is crucial to analyze trends in high school SRCs to guide prevention efforts and ensure the safety of adolescents. Prior studies indicate that high school girls participat - ing in sports comparable to those played by boys have a 2-times-higher SRC injury rate. 3,8 Notably, research - ers consistently found a higher SRC injury rate in girls’ soccer, basketball, and softball versus comparable boys’ sports.3,8–11 Additionally, research indicates that SRCs constituted a higher proportion of all high school injuries among girls compared to boys.10 Recent evidence suggests that boys and girls exhibit differences in mechanism of SRC in comparable activities. 12 Girls more often incur their SRCs due to player-to–playing surface or player-to- equipment contact, whereas boys sustained the majority of their SRCs due to player-to-player contact.10,12,13 How- ever, with the global pandemic as well as decreasing and increasing sports participation over the past decade, it is important to continuously examine and document trends in SRCs between boys’ and girls’ high school sports. Beginning in the 2015/2016 season, the Michigan High School Athletic Association (MHSAA) requires all high schools to report all head injuries incurred during an MHSAA-sponsored practice or competition into their Head Injury Reporting System (HIRS).8 The data derived from this surveillance system established SRC prevalence, the number of SRCs relative to the number of participat - ing student-athletes in a given sport, and with continued surveillance enables researchers to gain valuable insight into patterns of head injuries across all high school sports in the state of Michigan. Therefore, the current study de- scribes the epidemiology of SRCs among 33 high school sports across 8 years (2015/2016–2022/2023). Our objec- tives were to 1) determine SRC clinical incidence across high school sports; 2) compare SRC clinical incidence between boys and girls in comparable sports; 3) describe trends in SRC clinical incidence across the study period; and 4) determine common mechanisms of injury within boys’ and girls’ sports. Based on previous literature, we hypothesized that we will observe higher SRC clinical incidence in girls relative to boys in comparable sports, that clinical incidence will remain stable across study years, and that there will be significant differences in SRC mechanisms between boys and girls in comparable sports. Comprehending the epidemiology of SRCs among adolescent athletes is imperative for developing effective, focused primary prevention initiatives in this population. Methods Schools and Participants Data were collected for a total of 8 years spanning the 2015/2016 to 2022/2023 academic years. MHSAA mem- ber schools remained consistent, with approximately 750 high schools reporting head injuries to the surveillance syst

Bretzin et al. Neurosurg Focus Volume 57 • July 2024 3 MHSAA staff continuously monitor HIRS data for er- rors and missing data and are the only individuals allowed to modify SRC reports. To ensure completeness of data entry, the MHSAA staff review follow-up reports on a weekly basis. MHSAA staff email each school that sub - mitted an initial report every 2–3 weeks to remind them to submit a final follow-up report. At the end of each sports season, schools with no head injury reports are mandated to report this absence in the HIRS. Follow-up procedures persisted throughout each season for schools that either had not reported any concussions or had reported zero concussions until data were obtained from no fewer than 99% of MHSAA member high schools. Statistical Analysis Descriptive data included frequencies and percentages of the number of athletic participants and the practice and competition SRCs for each sport for each academic year. We calculated the clinical incidence of SRC, dividing the number of SRCs by the number of athletic participants multiplied by 100 player-seasons, and presented data as 95% CIs. We conducted clinical incidence analyses over- all, and for boys’ and girls’ sports separately, and stratified by each academic year and also independently for each sport. We included data from 2019/2020 and 2020/2021; however, due to the COVID-19 pandemic we counsel cau- tion regarding interpretations. We calculated the overall clinical incidence among all sports, and for boys’ and girls’ sports with and without academic years impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic. To determine trends across academ- ic years, we also report the slope of each clinical incidence value within each sport and the associated p values, deter- mining significance at p < 0.05. We then calculated clinical incidence ratios (CIRs) and 95% CIs to compare clinical incidence of SRC between boys’ and girls’ teams in com- parable sports, but only among sports that had more than 50 SRCs across all academic years in the study period (i.e., baseball/softball, basketball, lacrosse, soccer, swim and dive, track and field), determining significance if 95% CIs excluded 1.00. We reported the frequencies of mechanism of injury overall for boys’ and girls’ teams and within indi- vidual sports for 2016/2017 through 2022/2023 because the first year of data collection combined contact with a sur - face and contact with an object into the same mechanism. We determined significant associations between boys’ and girls’ teams for comparable sports with more than 50 SRC cases by using chi-square analyses (p < 0.05). All analyses were completed in Stata version 17 (StataCorp). Neurosurg Focus Volume 57 • July 2024 8 SRC in Competition Versus Practice Overall, we observed that a higher percentage of all SRCs occurred during competition events, which aligns with previous research.5,18,36 Our descriptive data revealed unique within-sport patterns; more than 80% of SRC in ice hockey, lacrosse, and soccer occurred in competition events. In contrast, other sports (i.e., competitive cheer - leading, swimming and diving), exhibited a higher per - centage of SRCs occurring during practice sessions. This phenomenon may potentially be attributed to the training and practice protocols in competitive cheerleading and swimming and diving, in which repetitive movements or specific drills might heighten the risk of SRC during prac- tice sessions, contrasting with the more controlled environ- ment of structured competitions. In addition, high school competitive cheerleading often features fewer competi - tions throughout the year compared to other sports, which illustrates the benefit that more nuanced epidemiology methods to measure at-risk time during athletic activity may have in future research. Separately, in swimming and diving, the proximity of participants sharing lanes during practices or the repetitive dive routines may contribute to an increased risk of SRC occurrences, thus highlighting the need for unique sport-specific contexts in future SRC prevention initiatives. Limitations Limitations of our study include de-identified data; thus, we could not cluster by school or team in our clinical incidence analyses, which may influence the findings of this study. Second, our findings are limited to the clinical incidence of concussion based on total athlete participa - tion numbers within each sport, whereas future research may benefit from identifying an appropriate measure of exposure time. Finally, the sample was limited to student- athletes participating in school-sanctioned high school sports across Michigan. These factors could potentially limit the generalizability of findings to a broader national or international context, given that regional variations in sports culture, healthcare access, and policy could impact injury reporting and management as well as prevention strategies. Conclusions The findings of this large SRC epidemiology study le- veraging a statewide surveillance system offer continued insights into the clinical incidence of SRC among high school athletes. With a large and increasing number of adolescents participating in high school–sanctioned sports nationally, there is a pressing need for ongoing research to identify opportunities for targeted primary prevention of SRC. Our study identified 25,482 total SRCs, with an overall clinical incidence of 1.17 per 100 player-seasons across all years. Moreover, our study highlighted sport- specific SRC mechanisms, and identified mechanism dif- ferences between boys and girls in comparable activities, emphasizing the importance of tailored prevention strate- gies. Additionally, although competition settings generally comprised a higher percentage of SRCs, certain sports like competitive cheerleading and swimming and diving ex - hibited higher percentages during practice sessions. These insights underscore the need for continued research and targeted interventions to mitigate SRC risks in high school sports settings. The main aims of this thesis were to describe the epidemiology of adolescent footballers, to describe how growth and maturation are associated with injury risk in academy male players and to study the accuracy of methods to estimate somatic maturity status. WHY DID I DO? Injuries occurring during youth can negatively affect academy progression 1 and result in long- term health consequences.2 Growth and maturation represent two potential non- modifiable intrinsic risk factors that are unique to adolescent footballers. The liter- ature published on this topic is, however, contradic- tory and findings in earlier studies are inconsistent. 3 HOW DID I DO IT? This thesis analysed injury, anthropometric and skeletal age data from routine monitoring of players at Athletic Club, whose professional male team plays in Spanish La Liga (1997–2022). Injury classification was based on the consensus of the International Federation of Association Football 4 and practitioner’s experience. Individual exposure was recorded since the season of 2011–2012, which allowed us to describe injury incidence (number of injuries/exposure) and injury burden (number of days lost/exposure) for each injury in each category. Further, hand- wrist X - rays allow ed us to compare injury burden between relative skeletal maturity status groups (early, on- time, late maturer) in men under 14 players. Longitudinal height data allowed to calculate peak height velocity (PHV), age at PHV , adult stature and growth rate for each player. These metrics were used to classify players according to their maturity status (pre- PHV , circa- PHV and post- PHV), timing (early , on- time, late) ( figure 1) and growth rate (fast, average, slow) and describe the association of these variables with injury risk. In addition, maturity status assessment based on longi- tudinal height recording was used as a reference to study the accuracy by different maturity esti- mation methods (visual assessment of incomplete growth curves, maturity offset and ratio equations, percentage of predicted adult height (PAH%)). WHAT DID I FIND? 1. Injury patterns differed according to age- group category and genre. Knee joint/ligament injuries (in women’s teams) and growth- related injuries (in U15 and younger) showed the largest injury burden values. 2. Growth and maturation were associated with injury risk of Athletic Club male academy foot- ball players. i. Skeletal relative maturity status (early, on- time, late) was associated with different in - jury patterns in U14 male football players. Specifically, early maturers showed a high- er overall, muscle and joint/ligament injury burden. 5 ii. The occurrence 6 and impact 7 of specific injuries varied according to maturity status (pre- PHV , circa- PHV , post- PHV or adult). Growth- related injuries peaked in circa- PHV , while muscle and joint/ligament in- juries were more burdensome in post- PHV and specially, adult players. Distal injuries (eg, Sever’s disease) had a higher impact in pre- PHV , while proximal injuries (eg, spon- dylolysis) peaked in post- PHV . iii. Players with a fast PHV (≥10.84 cm/year) showed a higher growth- related injury burden in circa- PHV .8 5. V isual assessment of the individual growth curves by an ex- perienced assessor was the method with the highest accura- cy to classify players as pre- PHV , circa- PHV or post- PHV . Key strengths of the study were the opportunity to follow a large number of FBS universities during the 16-year period, using prospective, validated methods that reduced fluctuations often observed in single- season injury patterns and individual team effect, 76,77 as well as minimized the over- and underestimation of sport trauma observed in publicly obtained data- bases. 71,73,78 In addition, the combined method of assessing functional outcome, direct observation, and treatment records as well as the daily interac- tions of ATCs in direct communication with athletes in this study minimized the potential for transfer bias and unreported injuries throughout the season. 29,70 In totality, these efforts enhanced the ability to iden- tify adductor-related groin injury incidence and possi- ble differences between artificial and natural grass fields. The influence of risk factors other than an artificial turf versus natural grass field cannot be overlooked. Because of inherent challenges of collecting data on multiple indices and on numerous teams and players over an extended period of time, the degree of influ- ence from these risk factors remains a limitation that can only be acknowledged at this time 16,70 However, the prospective cohort multivariate design enhanced sample size, controlled for seasonal and team varia- tion, and allowed for greater insight into the subtle dif- ferences in adductor-related groin injuries at the collegiate level of play. CONCLUSION In collegiate football, heavyweight artificial turf was found to be as safe as natural grass with respect to adductor-related groin injuries. The hypothesis that surface type would not affect groin injury rates was sup- ported, with no meaningful difference in injury incidence between artificial and natural grass surfaces. Further research is warranted to elucidate the link between groin trauma and long-term adverse health outcomes and to determine if these results are generalizable to other levels of football competition. My third study 12 included a large- scale cluster - randomised controlled trial that investigated the efficacy of the ‘FUNBALL ’ programme in male youth football players. A total of 1027 players from Kosovo who were competing in the Under (U) 15, U17 and U19 age groups were randomised either into the intervention or control group. Both groups were followed for one football season (August 2021–May 2022). My fourth study 13 was a secondary analysis of the data collected in the second study, which evaluated the epidemiology of football- related injuries in players of the control arm who were not exposed to the ‘FUNBALL ’ programme. WHAT DID I FIND? My first study indicated that the treatment effect associated with the use of multi- component ex ercise- based IPPs in football is uncertain and inconclusive (figure 1). This conclusion was based on the observation that the PI values crossed ‘1’, which marks the programme’s cut- off point for being either protective (<1) or indicative of increased injury risk (>1). Also, the results were mainly based on very low and low quality of evidence. According to my third study, the ‘FUNBALL ’ programme reduced the incidence rate for the overall number of time- loss injuries by 31% (IRR 0.69, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.87, p=0.002) when it was implemented for one football season. Injury burden was nearly halved in the intervention group (40 vs 74 days lost per 1000 hours). The key finding from my fourth study was a lower injury incidence in youth players compared with adult players. The most commonly injured body regions (thigh, knee and ankle) comprised 64% of all injuries in the male players aged 13–19 years. We observed a higher injury incidence in the older age groups. A total of four articles were included in the thesis. My first study (a systematic review and meta- analysis)6 examined the efficacy of multi- component exercise- based IPP s on reducing football- related injuries among footballers of all age groups. 15 studies (n=22 177 players) were included in the analysis. It described the developmental process of the ‘FUNBALL ’ programme, including the rationale, end- user involvement (eg, coach and football feder- ation administrators) and the iterative design and piloting steps. The ‘FUNBALL ’ programme was developed specifically for youth (aged 13–19 years) footballers with end- users, to be used after the usual warm- up. It aimed to address known implementa - tion barriers, such as a lack of football relevance, time and player/coach enjoyment. 9 This is achieved through the inclusion of ‘FUN’ activities to better address the barrier of player and coach engagement, particularly for youth age groups. The ‘FUNBALL ’ programme includes six mandatory exercise cate- gories and one optional category of games. Exer - cise categories were evidence- based,10 and each included two different exercises, which coaches were free to choose. All exercises were organised into progressive levels of difficulty. The ‘FUNBALL ’ programme incorporated exercises that allow for competition between players. WHAT DID I FIND? My first study indicated that the treatment effect associated with the use of multi- component ex ercise- based IPPs in football is uncertain and inconclusive (figure 1). This conclusion was based on the observation that the PI values crossed ‘1’, which marks the programme’s cut- off point for being either protective (<1) or indicative of increased injury risk (>1). Also, the results were mainly based on very low and low quality of evidence. According to my third study, the ‘FUNBALL ’ programme reduced the incidence rate for the overall number of time- loss injuries by 31% (IRR 0.69, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.87, p=0.002) when it was implemented for one football season. Thigh injury incidence was reduced by 38% (IRR 0.62, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.98, p=0.042); moderate injuries (time- loss between 7 and 28 days) were reduced by 35% (IRR 0.65, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.97, p=0.035) and severe injuries (time- loss >28 days) were reduced by 49% (IRR 0.51, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.91, p=0.024). Injury burden was nearly halved in the intervention group (40 vs 74 days lost per 1000 hours). The key finding from my fourth study was a lower injury incidence in youth players compared with adult players. The most commonly injured body regions (thigh, knee and ankle) comprised 64% of all injuries in the male players aged 13–19 years. We observed a higher injury incidence in the older age groups. WHAT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL FINDING? Based on the third study, the ‘FUNBALL ’ programme reduced overall time- loss injury incidence in male youth football players and was most effective for thigh injuries. The programme contained more football- specific elements compared with existing IPPs, which may increase implementation of the ‘FUNBALL ’ programme.
